title: Group 1 - The Alkali Metals
content:
# Group 1 - The Alkali Metals

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the properties of Group 1 elements
- Explain the trend in reactivity down the group
- Write equations for reactions with water and oxygen
- Explain observations in terms of electronic structure

## Introduction

The **alkali metals** (Group 1) are lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, and francium. They are the most reactive metals and must be stored under oil to prevent reaction with air and moisture.

## Key Concepts

### Group 1 Elements

| Element | Symbol | Atomic number | Configuration | Melting point (°C) |
|---------|--------|---------------|---------------|--------------------|
| Lithium | Li | 3 | 2,1 | 181 |
| Sodium | Na | 11 | 2,8,1 | 98 |
| Potassium | K | 19 | 2,8,8,1 | 63 |
| Rubidium | Rb | 37 | 2,8,18,8,1 | 39 |
| Caesium | Cs | 55 | 2,8,18,18,8,1 | 29 |

### Physical Properties

| Property | Description | Comparison to other metals |
|----------|-------------|---------------------------|
| Density | Low | Float on water (Li, Na, K) |
| Melting point | Low | Can be cut with knife |
| Hardness | Soft | Get softer going down |
| Appearance | Shiny when cut | Tarnish quickly in air |
| Conductivity | Good | Conduct electricity |

**Trends going down the group:**
- Melting point **decreases**
- Density **increases** (but Li, Na, K still float on water)
- Hardness **decreases** (easier to cut)
- Atomic radius **increases**
- Reactivity **increases**

### Why Are They So Reactive?

**All Group 1 elements:**
- Have **1 electron** in their outer shell
- Easily **lose this electron** to form +1 ions
- Achieve stable noble gas configuration

$$\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{Na}^+ + \text{e}^-$$

**Why does reactivity increase down the group?**
- Atoms get larger down the group
- Outer electron is further from nucleus
- More shielding from inner electrons
- Less attraction between nucleus and outer electron
- Outer electron is lost more easily
- Reaction is faster and more vigorous

### Reaction with Water

**General equation:**
$$\text{2M} + \text{2H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{2MOH} + \text{H}_2$$

(Where M = alkali metal)

**Specific equations:**
$$\text{2Li} + \text{2H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{2LiOH} + \text{H}_2$$
$$\text{2Na} + \text{2H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{2NaOH} + \text{H}_2$$
$$\text{2K} + \text{2H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{2KOH} + \text{H}_2$$

### Observations with Water

| Metal | Observations |
|-------|---------------|
| Lithium | Floats, fizzes steadily, moves around, slowly gets smaller |
| Sodium | Floats, fizzes vigorously, melts into ball, moves rapidly, may ignite (yellow flame) |
| Potassium | Floats, fizzes violently, ignites immediately (lilac flame), may explode, moves erratically |

[DIAGRAM: Sodium reacting with water - ball of metal floating, fizzing, moving across surface]

**Products:**
- Metal hydroxide solution (alkaline, pH > 7)
- Hydrogen gas (squeaky pop test)

**Why do they float?**
- Density less than water (for Li, Na, K)
- Also, hydrogen bubbles lift them

**Why do they melt?**
- Reaction is exothermic
- Low melting points
- Heat released melts the metal

### Reaction with Oxygen

**General equation:**
$$\text{4M} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{2M}_2\text{O}$$

**Specific equations:**
$$\text{4Li} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{2Li}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{4Na} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{2Na}_2\text{O}$$

**Observations:**
- Metals tarnish quickly (lose shine)
- Burn with characteristic flame colours:
  - Lithium: **red**
  - Sodium: **yellow**
  - Potassium: **lilac**

### Reaction with Chlorine

$$\text{2M} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{2MCl}$$

**Example:**
$$\text{2Na} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{2NaCl}$$

- Vigorous reaction
- White smoke (metal chloride)
- Ionic compound formed

### Storage and Safety

**Why stored under oil:**
- Prevents contact with air (oxygen) and moisture
- Stops tarnishing and reaction

**Safety precautions:**
- Handle with forceps (never touch)
- Use small pieces only
- Safety screens for K, Rb, Cs
- Never dispose of in bin or sink

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Describe what you would observe when a small piece of potassium is added to water.

**Solution:**
- Potassium floats on the water
- It melts into a silvery ball
- It moves rapidly/erratically across the surface
- Vigorous fizzing/effervescence
- It catches fire with a lilac flame
- It may explode at the end
- The water becomes alkaline (hydroxide formed)

---

**Example 2:** Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium.

**Solution:**
- Potassium has more electron shells than sodium (4 vs 3)
- The outer electron is further from the nucleus
- There is more shielding from inner electrons
- The outer electron experiences less attraction to the nucleus
- The outer electron is lost more easily in potassium
- Therefore, potassium reacts more vigorously

---

**Example 3:** Write the equation for the reaction of lithium with water and name the products.

**Solution:**
$$\text{2Li} + \text{2H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{2LiOH} + \text{H}_2$$

Products: **Lithium hydroxide** and **hydrogen gas**

---

**Example 4:** Explain why alkali metals are stored under oil.

**Solution:**
- Alkali metals are very reactive
- They react with oxygen in the air (tarnish)
- They react with water vapour in the air
- Oil creates a barrier between the metal and air/moisture
- This prevents unwanted reactions
- The metals stay shiny and unreacted

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Thinking reactivity decreases down Group 1
- **Correct:** Reactivity INCREASES down Group 1

- **Mistake:** Writing NaOH₂ or similar wrong formulae
- **Correct:** Products are MOH (one hydroxide ion per metal)

- **Mistake:** Forgetting to balance equations (e.g., Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂)
- **Correct:** 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

## Practice Questions

1. State three physical properties of alkali metals. (3 marks)

2. Write a balanced equation for the reaction of sodium with water. (2 marks)

3. Describe and explain the trend in reactivity of Group 1 metals going down the group. (4 marks)

4. Compare the reactions of lithium and potassium with water. Include observations for each. (4 marks)

5. Explain why alkali metals:
   a) Form +1 ions (2 marks)
   b) Are stored under oil (2 marks)

6. Predict the observations when rubidium is added to water. Justify your predictions. (4 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Alkali metals | Group 1 elements (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) |
| Reactivity | How vigorously an element reacts |
| Shielding | The blocking effect of inner electrons |
| Tarnish | To lose shine due to reaction with air |

## Summary

- **Group 1** = Alkali metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr
- **Physical properties:** Soft, low density, low melting point, good conductors
- **1 outer electron** → lose it to form M⁺ ions
- **Reactivity increases down the group** (outer electron further from nucleus)
- **Reaction with water:** 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂
  - Produces metal hydroxide (alkaline) + hydrogen
- **Observations increase down group:** fizzing → melting → igniting → exploding
- **Stored under oil** to prevent reaction with air and water
- **Flame colours:** Li = red, Na = yellow, K = lilac
